title: Active Scanning
content: Adversaries probe victim infrastructure with active network traffic before an intrusion, in contrast to passive collection of public information. Scanning reveals which hosts are reachable, which services listen on which ports, and which software versions are exposed. The traffic is directed at the target rather than at a third-party dataset, so it is visible in perimeter firewall, IDS and web server logs. Detection focuses on connection attempts across many ports or addresses from a single source in a short window. Scanning alone is not an intrusion, but it frequently precedes exploitation attempts against the services it discovers.

title: Active Scanning: Scanning IP Blocks
content: Adversaries sweep ranges of IP addresses to learn which addresses are in use and which respond. Techniques include ICMP echo sweeps and TCP or UDP connection attempts across a contiguous address block. The resulting map of live hosts guides later, more targeted scanning. In logs this appears as a single source contacting many sequential addresses within one subnet.

title: Active Scanning: Vulnerability Scanning
content: Adversaries check exposed services for configurations and software versions known to be vulnerable. Scanners commonly fingerprint banners, request known paths, or send probe payloads that reveal whether a defect is present without fully exploiting it. Web server logs often show bursts of requests to unusual paths, and identifiable scanner user-agent strings may be present. A vulnerability scan against an internet-facing service is a strong precursor signal for an exploitation attempt.

title: Network Service Discovery
content: Adversaries enumerate services running on remote hosts, usually after they already have some access to the network. Port scanning from an internal host is a common form and is more significant than external scanning because it indicates a foothold already exists. Detection relies on internal flow records showing a workstation contacting many peers or many ports, which is unusual for normal endpoint behaviour. This activity often bridges initial access and lateral movement.

title: Account Discovery
content: Adversaries enumerate local, domain or cloud accounts to identify targets for credential access and privilege escalation. Enumeration may use built-in operating system utilities, directory service queries, or cloud provider APIs. Because the same commands are used by administrators, detection depends on context such as the account performing the query and whether it normally does so.

title: Phishing
content: Adversaries send fraudulent messages to obtain credentials or to induce execution of malicious content. Phishing may be broad and untargeted or narrowly tailored to an individual or role, which is known as spearphishing. Messages commonly impersonate a trusted brand or colleague, create urgency, and direct the recipient to a credential-harvesting page or an attachment. Analysis should preserve full message headers, because the visible display name is trivially forged while the delivery path and authentication results are not. Failed SPF, DKIM or DMARC checks, a reply-to address differing from the sender, and a recently registered link domain are all supporting indicators.

title: Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment
content: Adversaries attach a malicious file to a targeted email and rely on the recipient opening it. Common carriers include office documents with macros, archive files containing scripts or shortcuts, and installers disguised as invoices or reports. Execution usually requires the user to bypass a security warning, so awareness controls and macro restrictions materially reduce success. Mail gateway logs and endpoint process trees showing an office application spawning a script interpreter are primary detection sources.

title: Phishing: Spearphishing Link
content: Adversaries include a link in a targeted email rather than an attachment, so no malicious file traverses the mail gateway. The linked page typically imitates a familiar login portal to harvest credentials, or delivers a payload on visit. Indicators include a display text that does not match the underlying href, a lookalike or newly registered domain, and URL shorteners that hide the destination. Investigation should determine not only who received the message but who clicked and who submitted credentials.

title: Exploit Public-Facing Application
content: Adversaries exploit a weakness in an internet-facing application to gain access to the host or the data behind it. Common classes include injection defects, deserialisation flaws, authentication bypasses and file upload weaknesses. Web application and database logs frequently contain the payload itself, which makes them the primary evidence source. Reducing exposed surface, patching promptly and running applications with least privilege limit both the likelihood and the impact of this technique.

title: Valid Accounts
content: Adversaries use legitimate credentials to access systems, which makes their activity blend with normal operations. Valid accounts support initial access, persistence, privilege escalation and defence evasion simultaneously, because authorised sessions bypass many detections. Signals of misuse are contextual rather than signature based: sign-in from an unfamiliar location or device, access at an unusual time, or activity inconsistent with the account role. Multi-factor authentication and conditional access substantially raise the cost of this technique.

title: External Remote Services
content: Adversaries abuse externally reachable remote access services such as VPN concentrators, remote desktop gateways and management interfaces. These services accept authentication from the internet by design, so exposed instances attract both credential guessing and exploitation. Restricting access to known networks, enforcing multi-factor authentication and monitoring authentication volume are the principal controls.

title: User Execution
content: Adversaries rely on a user taking an action that runs malicious code, such as opening a file or following a link. The technique depends on social engineering rather than a software defect, so patching does not remove it. Endpoint telemetry showing a document, browser or mail client spawning a script interpreter or unexpected binary is the strongest detection signal.

title: User Execution: Malicious Link
content: A user follows an adversary-supplied link that leads to code execution or credential capture. This step usually follows a phishing message and precedes credential access or payload delivery. Proxy and DNS logs establish whether the link was actually visited, which distinguishes an attempted campaign from a successful one.

title: User Execution: Malicious File
content: A user opens an adversary-supplied file that executes code, commonly a document with macros, a script, a shortcut file or a disguised executable. The file hash and the resulting process tree are the core artefacts for scoping the intrusion. Searching the estate for the same hash reveals other recipients who may already have executed it.

title: Command and Scripting Interpreter
content: Adversaries execute commands through interpreters such as PowerShell, Windows command shell, Unix shells, or scripting runtimes. Because interpreters are legitimate and preinstalled, the technique supports living-off-the-land operations with no additional tooling. Detection depends on command-line logging and script block logging rather than file signatures, and on identifying encoded or obfuscated arguments.

title: Brute Force
content: Adversaries attempt to obtain credentials by systematically guessing them when they have no prior knowledge of the password. The characteristic signal is a high volume of authentication failures concentrated on one account, one source, or one service within a short interval. A successful authentication immediately following a burst of failures from the same source is a strong indicator of compromise and should be treated as such until disproved. Effective controls include account lockout or throttling, rate limiting at the network edge, multi-factor authentication, and monitoring for authentication failure spikes. Investigation should always determine whether any attempt succeeded, not merely that attempts occurred.

title: Brute Force: Password Guessing
content: Adversaries guess many passwords against one account without prior knowledge of the credential. Guesses often come from common password lists or from information about the target. The pattern is many failures for a single username, which account lockout policies are specifically designed to interrupt.

title: Brute Force: Password Spraying
content: Adversaries try a small number of commonly used passwords against many accounts, deliberately staying below lockout thresholds. Because failures are spread thinly across accounts, per-account monitoring misses the pattern entirely. Detection requires aggregation across the directory, looking for one source producing single failures against many distinct usernames.

title: Brute Force: Credential Stuffing
content: Adversaries replay username and password pairs stolen from unrelated breaches, exploiting password reuse. Success rates per attempt are low but the volume is high and the credentials are valid somewhere, so a proportion of attempts succeed outright. Indicators include distributed sources, high request volume against the login endpoint, and successful logins from addresses with no prior history for that account.

title: OS Credential Dumping
content: Adversaries extract credential material such as password hashes or plaintext secrets from operating system memory and credential stores. On Windows this frequently involves access to the LSASS process or to the SAM and NTDS databases. Successful dumping typically converts a single compromised host into estate-wide access, so it is a high-impact event. Detection focuses on unusual process access to credential stores and on known tooling behaviour rather than on file names.

title: Credentials from Password Stores
content: Adversaries retrieve credentials saved in browsers, password managers and operating system keychains. These stores concentrate high-value secrets in predictable locations, which makes them efficient targets after initial access. Monitoring for processes reading browser credential databases, and requiring re-authentication for vault access, are the practical controls.

title: Unsecured Credentials
content: Adversaries search for credentials stored insecurely in configuration files, scripts, source code repositories, command histories and cloud instance metadata. No exploitation is required because the secret is simply readable. Prevention relies on secret management systems, pre-commit scanning and rotating any credential that has ever been written to a file or a log.

title: Input Capture
content: Adversaries capture user input to obtain credentials, using keylogging, credential prompts that imitate legitimate dialogs, or interception of web forms. Captured input yields credentials that no password policy can protect. Detection focuses on unexpected hooks into input APIs and on unauthorised software installation.

title: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
content: Adversaries exploit a software defect to obtain higher privileges on a system they already have access to. Kernel drivers and privileged services are the usual targets because they run with elevated rights. Successful escalation invalidates host-level containment assumptions and should raise incident severity. Patching, exploit mitigations and least-privilege service accounts are the primary defences.

title: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism
content: Adversaries bypass or abuse the mechanisms intended to control elevation, such as user account control, sudo configuration or setuid binaries. No software defect is necessarily required; misconfiguration is often sufficient. Auditing sudo rules and elevation prompts, and alerting on privilege changes, are the practical controls.

title: Access Token Manipulation
content: Adversaries manipulate access tokens to run processes under a different security context than the one they authenticated with. This both escalates privilege and confuses attribution, because subsequent actions appear to belong to another account. Detection depends on process-level auditing of token operations rather than on authentication logs.

title: Scheduled Task/Job
content: Adversaries schedule tasks or jobs to run code at a chosen time or on system start, providing persistence and sometimes privilege escalation. The mechanism is legitimate and widely used by administrators, so detection depends on baselining which tasks should exist. Newly created tasks that invoke script interpreters or write to unusual paths deserve investigation.

title: Create Account
content: Adversaries create local, domain or cloud accounts to retain access independently of any credential the defender may reset. An account created outside the normal provisioning process is a high-fidelity indicator, because legitimate account creation almost always has a corresponding ticket or workflow record. Reviewing recently created accounts is a standard step when scoping an intrusion.

title: Indicator Removal
content: Adversaries delete or alter logs, command histories and files to hinder detection and investigation. Cleared event logs and truncated histories are themselves evidence, because legitimate operations rarely produce them. Forwarding logs to a separate system that the compromised host cannot modify is the effective countermeasure.

title: Obfuscated Files or Information
content: Adversaries encode, encrypt, pack or otherwise obscure payloads and commands to defeat signature-based inspection. Base64-encoded command lines, packed binaries and password-protected archives are common forms. Detection shifts from content signatures to behavioural indicators such as an interpreter decoding a long argument at runtime.

title: Data from Information Repositories
content: Adversaries mine internal repositories such as wikis, ticketing systems, code repositories and file shares for valuable data and for credentials embedded in documentation. Access is often through legitimate accounts, so volume and breadth of access are the discriminating signals. Bulk retrieval outside a user role is a common insider-threat indicator as well.

title: Data from Local System
content: Adversaries gather files and data from a compromised host prior to exfiltration, often staging them into a single archive first. The appearance of a large archive in a temporary directory shortly before outbound transfer is a recognisable staging pattern. Correlating collection with a subsequent transfer establishes the exfiltration sequence.

title: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
content: Adversaries send collected data out over the same channel already used for command and control, avoiding a second, separately detectable connection. Detection focuses on the ratio of outbound to inbound bytes on a session, on beaconing regularity, and on destinations with no business relationship. Network flow records rather than payload inspection usually provide the evidence.

title: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
content: Adversaries move data out using a protocol different from the command-and-control channel, such as DNS, FTP or SMTP. Protocol misuse of this kind often evades controls tuned only to web traffic. Unusually large or frequent DNS queries with encoded subdomains are a classic indicator.

title: Exfiltration Over Web Service
content: Adversaries upload data to legitimate cloud storage, code hosting or paste services, so the destination is a reputable domain that blocklists will not catch. The traffic is encrypted and indistinguishable from normal use of the same service. Controls rely on data loss prevention, on restricting unsanctioned services, and on alerting when upload volume for an account departs from its baseline.

title: Data Transfer Size Limits
content: Adversaries split exfiltrated data into small chunks to stay under volume-based alerting thresholds. Because no single transfer looks anomalous, detection requires aggregating transfer volume per host or account over a longer window. Regular, similarly sized outbound transfers to one destination are the pattern to look for.

title: Network Denial of Service
content: Adversaries exhaust network bandwidth or infrastructure capacity to make a service unavailable to legitimate users. Volumetric floods and reflection or amplification attacks are the common forms, and traffic frequently originates from many distributed sources. Because saturation occurs upstream of the target, effective mitigation requires cooperation with the network provider or a scrubbing service rather than local filtering alone. Characterising the traffic by protocol, source distribution and request pattern is the first response step.

title: Endpoint Denial of Service
content: Adversaries exhaust the resources of a specific service or application rather than the network link, for example by consuming connection tables, worker threads or application state. Attack volume can be modest while still being effective, which distinguishes it from volumetric flooding. Rate limiting, connection timeouts and resource quotas at the application layer are the relevant controls.

title: Data Encrypted for Impact
content: Adversaries encrypt data in place to deny access to it, which is the defining behaviour of ransomware. Encryption is usually preceded by credential theft, lateral movement and deliberate destruction of backups and shadow copies. Detection signals include mass file modification, rapid entropy change across a share, and deletion of recovery points. Tested offline backups remain the control that most reliably determines the outcome.

title: Data Destruction
content: Adversaries irrecoverably delete or overwrite files and storage to disrupt operations, sometimes to destroy evidence of prior activity. Unlike ransomware there is no recovery path through payment, so backup integrity is the only remedy. Mass deletion events and use of secure-wipe utilities are the detection signals.
